client: I’ve been assigned a major group project at university, and it’s making me really anxious. I keep worrying about having to present in front of everyone, and the thought of speaking up in group discussions makes me freeze up. I’m not sure if therapy can really help with this—it feels like something I just have to deal with on my own.
therapist: It sounds like this project is bringing up a lot of anxiety for you, especially around speaking up in groups. That can feel really overwhelming when your mind starts anticipating the worst. What kind of thoughts come up when you imagine yourself in those group discussions?

client: I just keep thinking that everyone will judge me if I say something wrong or if my ideas aren’t good enough. I imagine them thinking I’m awkward or not smart enough to contribute. It’s hard to shake that feeling, and it makes me want to avoid saying anything at all. I don’t know if therapy can really change how I feel in those moments—it’s like my mind just takes over.
therapist: It sounds like those feelings of judgment and self-doubt are really sticking with you, even though they’re causing you to pull back from contributing. That’s a tough spot to be in. What do you think might happen if you challenged those thoughts—like, what evidence do you have that people would judge you harshly?

client: I guess there isn't really evidence... but that's the problem, I don't know what they're thinking. When I look back, people have been nice when I've spoken up before, but I still feel like they're just being polite. It's hard to trust that they actually mean it. I don't know how to stop assuming the worst when I can't read their minds.
therapist: It sounds like even when people respond positively, it’s hard to take that at face value—like there’s always a lingering doubt. That uncertainty can feel really unsettling. What do you think it would mean about you if someone *was* judging you negatively? What’s the worst-case scenario in your mind?

client: If someone was judging me negatively, it would probably mean I’m not good enough or that I don’t belong in the group. The worst-case scenario is that they’d think I’m awkward or not smart enough, and maybe they’d stop wanting to work with me. It feels like it’s confirming something I already believe about myself—that I’m not capable. I don’t know how to stop feeling that way.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a deep worry here that others’ judgments might confirm your own doubts about yourself—like it’s not just about the group project, but something bigger. That’s a really heavy weight to carry into these situations. What would it take for you to start challenging that belief that you’re "not capable"? What small evidence might point in a different direction?

client: I guess I have done okay in other group projects before, even if I felt anxious. But it’s hard to focus on those moments because my mind keeps going back to the times I felt judged or didn’t speak up. I don’t know how to trust the positive experiences—it’s like they don’t count as much as the negative ones. It feels like I’m always waiting for the next time I’ll mess up.
therapist: It makes sense that the negative experiences stick with you more—our minds tend to hold onto those harder, like they’re louder than the positive ones. But I notice you *did* mention doing okay in other projects—that’s important, even if it doesn’t feel as strong right now. What would it look like to give those positive moments a little more weight, even just as an experiment?

client: I guess I could try to focus on the positive moments, but it feels like forcing myself to think differently won’t really change how I feel in the moment. When I’m in a group setting, the anxiety just takes over, and it’s hard to remember anything good. I’m not sure how to make those positive experiences feel real when I’m feeling so overwhelmed.
therapist: It sounds like the anxiety in those moments is so intense that it overshadows any past positive experiences—like your brain goes into survival mode. That’s really tough to work against in the moment. What if we tried breaking it down: what’s one small, manageable step you could take to test whether focusing on a positive moment *could* shift things, even just a little?

client: I could try writing down one positive experience before the next group meeting, but I'm not sure it'll help in the moment when my heart starts racing. It feels like a drop in the ocean compared to the anxiety that takes over. What if I look at the note and still feel just as panicked? Then I'll feel even worse for failing at this too.
therapist: It sounds like you're already anticipating that this experiment might not work—and that fear of it "failing" is adding even more pressure. That’s completely understandable when anxiety feels so overpowering. But what if we framed it differently: what would it mean if you looked at the note and still felt panicked, but you kept trying anyway? Could that be its own kind of success?

client: I guess trying anyway would mean I didn't let the panic completely stop me, but it still feels like I'm lying to myself if I don't actually feel better. Why should I have to force myself through something that feels so awful? It's exhausting pretending things are okay when they're not.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a real frustration building—like you’re tired of pushing through the anxiety while feeling like you’re just pretending. That exhaustion is completely valid. What if we shifted focus from "feeling better" to simply noticing what happens when you try, without judging whether it "worked" or not? Could there be value in observing the struggle itself?

client: Observing the struggle instead of judging it feels... different. I guess I’ve always been so focused on whether I’m "doing it right" that I never stopped to just notice what’s happening. But it’s hard to separate myself from the anxiety—it feels like it’s all-consuming. How do I even start observing without getting sucked back into the fear?
therapist: It sounds like you’re starting to consider a new way of approaching this, which is a big step—but I hear how overwhelming it feels to shift away from judging yourself. When you say the anxiety feels "all-consuming," it’s clear how much space it takes up in your mind. What would it feel like to take just one moment—even a tiny one—to notice the anxiety without trying to fix it or judge it? Could that feel different than getting "sucked back in"?

client: Taking just one moment to notice the anxiety without judging it feels... strange. Like, if I’m not trying to fix it or push it away, what’s the point? I worry that if I stop fighting it, it’ll just take over even more. It’s hard to imagine that simply noticing it could make any difference.
therapist: It sounds like this idea of simply noticing the anxiety feels unfamiliar and even a bit unsettling—like stepping into uncharted territory. That’s completely natural when you’re used to fighting it head-on. What if we framed it this way: noticing isn’t about giving the anxiety power, but about creating a little space between you and it, so it doesn’t feel so overwhelming. What do you think might happen if you tried that, even just once?
